subject: english-literature
title: Voices of Now: Reading Contemporary British Poetry
welcome_lead: Explore the formal and thematic preoccupations of post-2000 British poetry as set by AQA — voice, identity, politics, and form.
meta_desc: A-Level AQA Post-2000 Poetry adventure: Duffy, Armitage, Heaney, voice and identity in contemporary verse.
final_note: Contemporary poetry rewards close attention to voice as much as to image — listen for who is speaking, and why.

concepts.def: A poem in the voice of a constructed speaker distinct from the poet; central to Duffy's 'The World's Wife' (1999) and her later work.
Verse without regular metre or rhyme; dominant in post-2000 collections but rarely unstructured — line breaks remain semantically charged.
First-person poetry foregrounding intimate, often autobiographical material; complicated in contemporary work by performative self-construction.
Engagement with race, gender, sexuality and class as constitutive of voice; central to Jay Bernard, Kayo Chingonyi, Imtiaz Dharker.
Poetry that responds to visual art; revived in contemporary verse as a means of meditation on representation.
The use of everyday, colloquial language; Armitage's signature register, blending Northern English with literary form.

walkthroughs.body_html: Carol Ann Duffy (Poet Laureate 2009–19) extends the Browning monologue into feminist territory. In Rapture (2005) the speaker is unstable, lyrical, and self-conscious. AQA responses should distinguish between speaker and poet, attending to irony, gaps, and self-betrayal. Duffy's typical strategy is to inhabit a perspective just long enough to expose its limits.

Simon Armitage (Laureate 2019–) writes in a deceptively plain Yorkshire register. Collections such as The Unaccompanied (2017) use loose pentameter and half-rhyme. The roughened metre dramatises ordinary speech under pressure. Critics note his Anglo-Saxon ear: Armitage has translated Sir Gawain and Pearl, and the alliterative tradition shadows his line.

Although his major work predates 2000, Seamus Heaney's District and Circle (2006) and Human Chain (2010) qualify. These collections meditate on post-9/11 anxiety, ageing, and Northern Irish memory. Heaney's late style compresses image and ethical weight: the bog-body poems of the 1970s give way to elegiac, civic verse.
